definition: Also called direct-to-chip: cooling that pipes liquid to cold plates on hot components (CPU/GPU) instead of relying on air. Covers roughly 100-175 kW/rack — the band above rear-door heat exchangers and below immersion. HPE ships fanless 100% DLC for top systems.

Submerging servers in a dielectric fluid (single- or two-phase) to remove heat. Used above roughly 175 kW/rack, where even direct-to-chip liquid cooling runs out of headroom. Enables extreme density but requires new mechanical/facility design.
The unit that circulates and controls coolant between the facility water loop and the server/rack liquid-cooling loop — the heart of a DLC deployment.

A liquid-cooled radiator mounted on the rack's back door that cools exhaust air, letting existing air-cooled racks handle higher density without full DLC. Stretches air-cooled racks to roughly 100 kW before direct-to-chip liquid becomes necessary.
Power drawn per rack. Traditional racks were 5-15 kW; AI racks (e.g., NVL72) now hit 100-140+ kW, forcing liquid cooling and data-center power/thermal redesign.
The heat (in watts) a cooling solution must dissipate for a chip at sustained load. Server CPU/GPU TDPs have climbed past 500W-1kW+, driving the shift to liquid cooling.
Ratio of total facility power to IT-equipment power. 1.0 is ideal; lower is more efficient. Liquid cooling and better design push PUE down, cutting energy cost and carbon.
Quick reference for which cooling method a rack needs: air works to ~20 kW, rear-door heat exchangers stretch to ~100 kW, direct-to-chip liquid covers ~100-175 kW, and above that you need immersion.

Fans blowing air through a rack work reliably up to roughly 20 kW/rack. Past that, the airflow volume needed to carry away the heat becomes impractical (noise, fan power, duct/floor space), forcing a move to rear-door heat exchangers or direct liquid cooling.

Liquid carries roughly 1000x the heat per unit volume that air does, and in direct-to-chip cooling it picks up heat right at the die instead of off a heatsink's surface. That's the physics behind the whole air -> rear-door -> direct-liquid -> immersion progression as rack power climbs.
Higher-voltage (48V vs 12V) rack/board power distribution that reduces current and resistive losses — increasingly standard (via OCP) for high-power AI racks.
